learningObjectives.title: The origins and value of the universe
The origins and value of human life

questions.q: Which scientific theory explains the origin of the universe?
questions.explain: Science explains the origin of the universe through the Big Bang, an explosion of matter and energy billions of years ago.

questions.q: How does Genesis 1:1 begin its account of creation?
options: 'In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth'
'God made humans in his own image'
'The earth was without form and void'
questions.explain: Genesis 1:1 opens the biblical creation account by stating that God created the heavens and the earth.

questions.q: What does the Christian concept of 'stewardship' teach about the environment?
options: Humans have a duty to look after and protect the world for God
Humans may use the earth's resources however they wish
The earth has no value because it will be destroyed
Only religious people should care for nature
questions.explain: Stewardship is the belief that humans have a God-given responsibility to care for and protect the earth.

questions.q: The idea that humans were given 'dominion' over the earth comes from which part of the Bible?
questions.explain: Genesis 1:28 records God telling humans to rule over, or have dominion over, the earth and its creatures.

questions.q: Why might experiencing 'awe and wonder' at the natural world strengthen religious belief?
options: It can be seen as evidence of a designer or creator God
It proves the Big Bang did not happen
It shows the universe has no purpose
It removes the need for scientific explanations
questions.explain: For many believers, the beauty and order of the universe inspire awe and point to a creator God behind it.

questions.q: A Christian recycles, reduces waste and campaigns against pollution. Which teaching best explains this behaviour?
questions.explain: Caring for the environment reflects stewardship, the duty to protect the world God created.

questions.q: What does 'sustainable development' mean?
options: Meeting present needs without harming future generations' ability to meet theirs
Using up resources as quickly as possible
Stopping all use of the earth's resources
questions.explain: Sustainable development uses resources in a way that does not damage the ability of future generations to meet their needs.

questions.q: Which scientific theory explains the origin and development of human life?
questions.explain: Science explains the origins of human life through Darwin's theory of evolution by natural selection.

questions.q: What does the Christian belief that humans are made 'in the image of God' (imago Dei) suggest?
options: Human life is special and has unique value
Humans look physically identical to God
Humans are the same as all other animals
questions.explain: Being made in God's image means humans have a special, God-given value that sets human life apart.

questions.q: What does the phrase 'sanctity of life' mean?
options: Life is holy and sacred because it is given by God
Life is only valuable if it is enjoyable
Life belongs to the individual to end when they choose
Human and animal life are of equal worth
questions.explain: Sanctity of life is the belief that life is holy and sacred because it is a gift from God.

questions.q: What is meant by 'quality of life'?
options: The extent to which a life is worth living or fulfilling
The length of a person's life in years
The amount of money a person has
The number of children a person has
questions.explain: Quality of life refers to how good and worthwhile a person's life is, rather than simply that they are alive.

questions.q: Many Christians believe that after death people will face which of the following?
options: A second physical birth on earth
questions.explain: Many Christians believe in resurrection followed by God's judgement, which affects how they live now.

questions.q: A believer argues that a terminally ill patient's life is still valuable simply because it was given by God. Which idea are they using?
questions.explain: Valuing life because it is God-given, regardless of suffering, is an appeal to the sanctity of life.

questions.q: In the UK, up to how many weeks is abortion generally legally permitted under the Abortion Act 1967?
questions.explain: The Abortion Act 1967, later amended, generally permits abortion up to 24 weeks of pregnancy.

questions.q: Which argument would most likely be used by someone who opposes abortion?
options: Life is sacred from the moment of conception
A woman has the right to choose
The foetus is not yet a person
Quality of life matters more than length of life
questions.explain: Opposition to abortion is often based on the sanctity of life, viewing the foetus as a sacred life from conception.

questions.q: A woman argues she should be able to end a pregnancy that resulted from rape. Which position does this reflect?
questions.explain: Emphasising a woman's right to decide, especially in difficult circumstances, is a pro-choice position.

questions.q: What is the current legal status of euthanasia in the United Kingdom?
options: It is legal for anyone over 18
It is legal only in hospitals
It is legal with a doctor's note
questions.explain: Euthanasia is against the law in the UK and can be treated as murder or manslaughter.

questions.q: What is meant by 'voluntary euthanasia'?
options: Ending a person's life at their own request
Ending life without the person's knowledge
Allowing someone to die of natural causes
questions.explain: Voluntary euthanasia is when a person's life is ended painlessly at their own clear request.

questions.q: A campaigner says a suffering, terminally ill patient should be allowed to die because their life is no longer worth living. Which idea supports this?
questions.explain: Arguing from suffering that a life is no longer worth living is an appeal to quality of life.

questions.q: Which belief might a Christian use to justify the responsible use of animals for food?
options: Animals have exactly the same rights as humans
All animals are sacred and must never be used
questions.explain: Genesis teaches that humans have dominion over animals, which some Christians use to justify their responsible use for food.

specSource: AQA GCSE Religious Studies A specification; Theme B: Religion & Life
